summary: Topic 5.3 explained the basis of genetics: patterns of inheritance which followed the findings of Gregor Mendel. Not all forms of inheritance follow the laws the Austrian observed, and Topic 5.4 is dedicated to explaining these Non-Mendelian patterns of inheritance.

vocab.definition: A form of Mendelian inheritance where one allele (the dominant allele) completely masks the effect of another allele (the recessive allele) for a specific trait
A genetic inheritance pattern where neither of two alleles is completely dominant or recessive, resulting in a blended or intermediate phenotype in the heterozygous individual
A genetic inheritance pattern where both alleles for a trait are fully and simultaneously expressed in the phenotype of a heterozygous individual
Three or more different versions of the same gene found within a population
Genes located on the same chromosome that tend to be inherited together due to their physical proximity, and do not independently assort
A diagram showing the relative positions and genetic distances between genes on a chromosome, based on the frequency of recombination (crossing over) during meiosis
Offspring whose allele combinations for specific genes are identical to the allele combinations of one of their parents
Offspring whose allele combinations for specific genes are not identical to the allele combinations of one of their parents
The inheritance of genes from structures other than the nucleus, such as the mitochondria
A gene located on one of the sex chromosomes, either the X or Y chromosome, which have unique patterns of inheritance due to the combinations of these chromosomes in different sexes
A diagram of a family tree that uses standardized symbols to show relationships and the inheritance of traits or genetic diseases across generations
